Tiafoe lost to fellow American Taylor Fritz two years later, when the U.S. came closest to ending it’s men’s drought.It certainly didn’t appear Tiafoe would be going back this time, after Michelsen continued his dominant run through his breakout tournament. He was the only man who hadn’t dropped a set, and he served to win the match with a 5-4 lead in the third.He couldn't finish it off and Tiafoe charged back after falling behind 3-0 in the fifth set.Tiafoe said his performance to start the match was slow and flat.“It wasn’t good, let’s put it that way. “Three out of five is a blessing, because you have time to get it together. I definitely waited for the last minute.”Tiafoe joined Andre Agassi as the only American men to reach three U.S. Open semifinals this century and will return to the top 10 for the first time in three years in the next rankings.Michelsen, ranked No. 46, fell to 0-6 in matches that go to a fifth set.

Postal Service from implementing Trump’s directive. Lucie County Fire Rescue also responded to the incident and the man was pronounced dead at the scene. "We will provide an update once there is new information to share." It remains unclear whether any suspicious items have been found or how long the search will take. Authorities have not released additional details about the source of the email threat. Parents were notified of the situation through a message from the school Thursday afternoon. No evidence of threat found In an update issued at 2:55 p.m., school officials said the Martin County Sheriff's Office was finalizing its sweep of the campus and found no evidence of a threat. Students and staff were cleared to return to their classrooms, and regular dismissal procedures were expected to continue as scheduled. Former President George W. Bush gave rare insight into his experience on Sept. came under attack by al-Qaida.Appearing with Condoleezza Rice, who served as his national security adviser, Bush spoke Wednesday from his presidential center two days before the 25th anniversary of the attacks.RELATED STORY | King Charles III and Queen Camilla honor 9/11 victims at Ground Zero in New YorkBush was at a Florida elementary school on the morning of the attacks. DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert and South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett, along with district board members Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr. Since entering its operational testing phase in May, the project has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes. Lambert said the project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year, and will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. "Florida's waterways are a deeply interconnected system and preventing these harmful discharges will further improve the health of the estuary and the lagoon," Lambert said. DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019 — a figure he said has never been matched in state history. He said his administration set an initial funding goal, beat it by nearly $1 billion in his first term, then set a second-term goal of $3.5 billion and has reached nearly $6 billion. The governor said his administration has completed or broken ground on more than 90 Everglades projects and has reached more project milestones than any previous administration in Florida history. He cited reductions of 5.6 million pounds of nitrogen per year and nearly 1 million pounds of phosphorus per year as among the tangible results of those investments. DeSantis also highlighted progress on the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir south of Lake Okeechobee, which he said was originally scheduled for completion in 2034. Through a partnership with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers announced after President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the project is now projected to be completed by 2029 and at nearly half the original federal cost estimate. "Isn't that something — what you want — under budget, ahead of schedule," DeSantis said. The EAA reservoir is designed to store 78 billion gallons of water and deliver 270 billion to 470 billion gallons of clean freshwater each year to the Everglades and Florida Bay. Bartlett said the pump station at the C-23 project site is capable of moving 166 million gallons of water every day — comparable in capacity to Miami's drinking water system — and has been operational since May 14. "We haven't had a lost summer since you've been in office, Governor," Bartlett said. "Have not had a lost summer." Lambert pointed to measurable environmental improvements since DeSantis took office, including seagrass returning to stable levels in the Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary, supporting fish and manatee populations as well as the ecotourism industry. The Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary are home to more than 4,000 species of plant and wildlife. DeSantis said the broader Everglades restoration effort is the largest and most ambitious restoration project in U.S. "When you think about America 250 — a massive country that spans a continent from sea to shining sea — there have been a lot of things that have been done over those 250 years, and there's never been a project of this magnitude that has been attempted, much less brought to fruition like we have," DeSantis said. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier was in West Palm Beach Thursday morning to announce the arrests of two alleged ringleaders in a coordinated baby formula theft operation that spanned multiple counties and resulted in over $1 million in stolen merchandise.Mohammed Alsaidi and Zeina Zabib, both of Lake Worth, were arrested on charges of conspiracy to commit racketeering and directing and dealing in stolen property. If convicted, they each face up to 90 years in prison.WATCH THE FULL PRESS CONFERENCE BELOW:The 15-month investigation, dubbed "Formula One," uncovered what authorities describe as a sophisticated criminal enterprise involving nearly a dozen individuals across six judicial circuits. The operation included more than 150 separate baby formula thefts from major retailers including Publix, Walmart, Target, Walgreens and CVS."This wasn't just a little bit of retail theft here or there," Uthmeier said. "This was a large, coordinated enterprise spanning over multiple counties and many circuits."Detective Christopher Apple of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office led the investigation. Apple explained that professional shoplifters, known as "boosters," stole baby formula and sold it to Alsaidi and Zabib, who acted as "fences" — purchasing the stolen goods and reselling them for profit at about five times what they paid.When authorities executed search warrants on Sept. 1, they found about 1,000 cans of baby formula worth about $38,000 in retail value in a warehouse in Davie that was not air-conditioned, along with 1,300 cans of tuna and sardines stored in temperatures exceeding 90 degrees.Nine other individuals have already been arrested in connection with the scheme, Uthmeier said.The arrests come as Florida has strengthened penalties for retail theft. Ron DeSantis signed HB 549, which allows repeat retail theft cases to be prosecuted as first-degree felonies carrying up to 30 years in prison.Uthmeier emphasized that retail theft is not a victimless crime, pointing to empty store shelves, increased security costs and higher prices for consumers as consequences of such operations."You don't want to upset moms ever. You certainly don't want to upset moms when it comes to feeding their little ones," Uthmeier said. "So, this is a fight that we will valiantly fight."

A former Fort Pierce police officer was arrested after investigators say he accessed Flock and other databases hundreds of times to track his ex-girlfriend. Josepher Crutchfield, who resigned from the Fort Pierce Police Department last month, was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts related to unauthorized computer access, according to the department. He was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on $80,000 secured bond. Flock cameras are license plate readers law enforcement can use to help identify vehicles connected to suspects in crimes. "The cameras are here for our community's safety, not to be abused by those who are entrusted to safeguarding," said Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith. Crutchfield had previously faced an Internal Affairs investigation over allegations of sexually inappropriate behavior toward female Fort Pierce police employees in 2021. Investigators said his behavior was excessive, unwelcome, and affected the employees' work environment. The department ultimately found he violated five policies and suspended him for two days without pay. The latest investigation began on Aug. 10, 2026 after the department was contacted by the media about concerns over possible misuse of its Flock automated license plate reader system. Crutchfield was placed on administrative leave on Aug. 7, 2026 and his access to law enforcement systems was revoked. A criminal investigation began Aug. Crutchfield resigned days later on Aug. 18 before the investigation was completed. Investigators later determined there was probable cause for his arrest. Chief Smith called the incident a black eye for the department. "The public places immense trust in those who wear this badge, and with that trust comes a tremendous responsibility. No one is above the law," he said. See also: Details of a Fort Pierce police officer's harassment that got him suspended without pay Between October 2025 and July 2026, Crutchfield allegedly accessed the Flock database 382 times to search the same license plate, using different reason categories and without a legitimate law enforcement purpose. Most of the searches were made while he was off duty. Investigators determined the vehicle was registered to an ex-girlfriend. The investigation expanded to other databases, including FCIC , NCIC , DAVID and TLO . Investigators found Crutchfield made additional searches over the last few years to look up people's names and personal information - searches that they said had no legitimate law enforcement purpose. Those databases contain restricted personal information, including addresses and dates of birth. Officers must acknowledge a warning each time they access the systems, confirming they are being used for legitimate law enforcement purposes. The chief said investigators are not speculating about Crutchfield's intentions or whether the alleged conduct amounted to stalking, but they will follow any additional leads. "The conduct alleged in this case is unacceptable and represents a serious breach of the trust that's placed in law enforcement," Smith said. " Again, it does not diminish the dedicated work that our officers do every day." The department has launched a broader audit of its law enforcement databases. So far, officials said no additional violations have been identified. Fort Pierce police have also tightened access to the Flock system. Only lieutenants and higher ranking officers can now use it, and each search requires approval from one of two deputy chiefs and a case number. Flock searches will be limited to forcible felony investigations and missing or endangered person cases. The department also cut its data retention period from 30 days to seven days. "The system will not be used for general investigative surveillance, intelligence gathering unrelated to an authorized investigation, or routine investigative inquiries," said Smith. Officials also added a position within the Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly audits of law enforcement databases. The chief acknowledged the incident is a setback for the department but said officials are committed to being transparent and holding officers accountable. "This is a black eye for the agency," the chief said. "This is a difficult moment for our organization and our community, but our responsibility is clear. The authority entrusted to police officers comes with an extraordinary responsibility. When there is criminal evidence that an officer may have violated the law, we have an obligation to act. The badge does not provide immunity from accountability."

Assuming each party wins the seats that currently lean in its favor, Republicans would need to win nine of the 21 House toss-ups and three of the six Senate toss-ups.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce commissioners give Kings Landing developers 180 days to find $15 million for Marriott hotel
hero.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday to give developers of the Kings Landing development 180 days to find $15 million in funding for the hotel portion of the project. Developers Live Oak and Main Sail say the Marriott hotel portion of the project will now cost around $65 million, $15 million more than previously planned. Earlier this summer, developers asked the city for the funds through a loan or grant, but were denied. Jon Collier with Main Sail said they will now look to secure the funds privately, telling officials they can get it done. A representative from Live Oak said the development team remains committed, noting they have millions of dollars invested and an enormous amount of time into the project and are extremely motivated to see it through to a successful completion.

The extension comes after developers missed a July 15 deadline to secure the funding for the project. Fort Pierce Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky voted against the extension, saying his opinion based on the legal review is that the city needs to stop now because doing another amendment continues to weaken the city's position and makes it more difficult to get the property back. Commissioner Michael Broderick, who voted for the extension, said taking back the property currently owned by Audubon Development would be costly and lead to litigation involving multiple parties. Broderick said everybody would be suing everybody, comparing it to having three fighters in the same ring who are all going to come out swinging at each other.

Broderick said the city has 30 days to draft a new amendment with developers, after which the six-month countdown will begin. When asked what happens if developers fail to find the money in time, Broderick said he would kick them to the curb and make the motion to terminate the deal. The commissioner's direct response signals a firm deadline for the developers to secure their financing or face termination of their agreement with the city.

Jon Nolli, who owns the Funky Cuda and other businesses in Fort Pierce and has a deposit on space in the Kings Landing development for a beer garden and deli, said he is cautiously watching the situation unfold. Nolli said if this is really what it takes and developers can find the money to do this, then everyone can move forward. However, he remains concerned about further delays, saying if this is just another step extending things along, it will be pretty tough on everybody involved in the project.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County sends 30-day removal notices to 50-55 license plate camera permit holders
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County has notified all automated license plate reader permit holders that they have 30 days to remove cameras from county rights-of-way. The county will remove non-compliant units itself if permit holders fail to act.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County sent letters earlier this week to all automated license plate reader permit holders, giving them 30 days to remove the cameras from county-maintained roads. Erick Gill, communications director for St. Lucie County, said the county issued about 50 to 55 permits for the cameras, including Flock cameras.

The letters went to permit holders that submitted permits on behalf of law enforcement agencies and directly to camera manufacturers. County rights-of-way include the shoulders of highways and roads maintained by the county. If permit holders fail to remove the cameras within the 30-day period, county staff will step in to remove them. Gill said permit owners will likely want to handle the removal themselves because the cameras have value and could be damaged, and the permit holders originally did the installations.

County staff provided the updates to commissioners during a meeting following a vote earlier this month. St. Lucie County residents expressed opposition to the surveillance cameras. Toria Hoke said she thinks the cameras are too intrusive and might impede freedom. Herman Felton said the cameras are spying on people, though he acknowledged they could be useful in certain situations. Felton raised concerns about privacy, saying people have a right to privacy and whatever they are doing at their house is their business.

County leaders clarified that the removal of the cameras from public roads does not mean they are banned entirely. Cameras can still be installed on private property or non-maintained rights-of-way.

hero.headline: Lake Worth man arrested after Martin County liquor theft, high-speed flight
hero.body:
A Lake Worth man is facing charges after he stole liquor from a Martin County store and drove recklessly through the area at speeds exceeding 80 mph before being arrested in Palm Beach County with help from a sheriff's helicopter.

Derwyn Don Edwards, 24, entered the Publix liquor store at 6805 SE Federal Highway around 11:24 a.m. and stole multiple bottles of liquor, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The retailer provided deputies with a description of Edwards and the vehicle he was driving.

A deputy located the vehicle near SE Dominica Terrace and Federal Highway and attempted a traffic stop, but Edwards failed to stop and continued driving recklessly, authorities said. Because the incident did not meet the agency's pursuit-policy criteria, the deputy turned off emergency lights and siren and disengaged. Edwards nevertheless continued driving dangerously, at times exceeding 80 mph, running red lights and endangering the public before heading south on Interstate 95, deputies said.

MCSO Air 1 located the vehicle and monitored it from above, guiding deputies as Edwards entered Palm Beach County without a ground pursuit. Edwards eventually parked and attempted to hide. Air 1 directed an unmarked unit to his location, and he was taken into custody with assistance from the Florida Highway Patrol. Edwards was charged with reckless fleeing and eluding and petit theft. He is being held at the Martin County Jail.

hero.headline: Plant City police login breach of Florida driver database revives stalled privacy bill
hero.body:
Hackers accessed Florida's driver database through a Plant City police employee's compromised login, renewing a Republican lawmaker's push to restrict third-party sales of motorist information ahead of the March 2027 legislative session.

The Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles said it learned of the breach Sept. 4 and contained it quickly. In a Sept. 11 statement, the agency attributed the intrusion to an international cybercriminal organization and said the employee's credentials had been improperly stored on a personal electronic device. The department notified the attorney general's office and is working with the Florida Digital Service and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement as the criminal investigation continues.

State Rep. Peggy Gossett-Seidman, R-Highland Beach, said the breach adds urgency to her effort to change how Florida handles motorist information. She wants agencies and businesses handling driver data to strengthen their safeguards. Her legislative push also addresses the legal sale and sharing of driver data. Gossett-Seidman wants an opt-out allowing drivers to block certain third-party sales while preserving access for law enforcement, insurance and vehicle recalls. Her earlier privacy proposal, HB 357, was filed in November 2025 for the 2026 legislative session but died in the Government Operations Subcommittee in March. An identical Senate bill sponsored by Sen. Alexis Calatayud also died in committee.

A 2019 investigation by Scripps reporter Adam Walser found Florida had sold information about drivers and state ID cardholders to more than 30 private companies. The sales generated more than $77 million in fiscal 2017 alone. Lakeland resident Sonia Arvin said her sister began receiving robocalls, direct-mail offers and visits from salespeople after obtaining a Florida ID. In response to that investigation, the state said companies buying the information were prohibited from using it for marketing and that it had stopped selling data to three companies since 2017 because of misuse. Gossett-Seidman said she has discussed another attempt with House leaders and Sen. Harrell and is hopeful the renewed attention to data privacy will help the proposal advance when Florida's regular legislative session begins March 2, 2027.

Deputies said Edwards nevertheless continued driving dangerously, at times exceeding 80 mph, running red lights and endangering the public before heading south on Interstate 95. MCSO Air 1 then located the vehicle and monitored it from above, guiding deputies as Edwards entered Palm Beach County without a ground pursuit. Authorities said Edwards eventually parked and attempted to hide. Air 1 directed an unmarked unit to his location, and he was taken into custody.

Edwards is being held at the Martin County Jail.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce commissioners vote 3-2 to give Kings Landing developers 180 days for hotel financing
hero.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday to give developers of the Kings Landing development 180 days to find $15 million in funding for the hotel portion of the downtown project.

Developers Live Oak and Main Sail say the Marriott hotel portion of the project will now cost around $65 million, which is $15 million more than previously planned. The extension comes after developers missed a July 15 deadline to secure the funding for the project. Earlier this summer, developers asked the city for the funds through a loan or grant but were denied. Jon Collier with Main Sail said they will now look to secure the funds privately.

Fort Pierce Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky voted against the extension. Dzadovsky said continuing to amend the deal continues to weaken the city's position and makes it more difficult to get the property back. Commissioner Michael Broderick, who voted for the extension, said taking back the property, which is currently owned by Audubon Development, would be costly and lead to litigation. Broderick said the city has 30 days to draft a new amendment with developers, after which the six-month countdown will begin. Broderick said if developers fail to find the money in time, he will make the motion to terminate the deal.

Jon Nolli, who owns the Funky Cuda and other businesses in Fort Pierce and has a deposit on space in the Kings Landing development for a beer garden and deli, said he is cautiously watching the situation unfold. Nolli said if developers can find the money, the project can move forward, but he remains concerned about further delays. A representative from Live Oak said the development team remains committed, noting millions of dollars invested and an enormous amount of time spent on the project.

hero.headline: Amazon to lay off nearly 500 workers at Port St. Lucie warehouse Sept. 17
hero.body:
Amazon will lay off close to 500 workers at its Port St. Lucie fulfillment center starting Thursday, September 17, according to a notice the company filed with the state. The filing lists roughly 494 employees who will be separated from the company, with separations effective September 17 and December 17. The job cuts are expected to be permanent.

Amazon filed the notice July 15 with Florida's State Trade and Rapid Response Coordinator and sent a copy to Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin under the federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act. The filing states operations will shut down at Amazon's PBI3 facility, 7600 LTC Pkwy, effective Thursday. Amazon told affected workers about the closure around June 18.

The vast majority of the affected positions, 466 of the 494, are FC Associate I roles, the facility's entry-level warehouse position. The rest include operations managers, HR staff, a safety specialist, an IT support associate and other roles. Affected employees aren't represented by a union and don't have seniority-based bumping rights to displace other workers. Amazon says it will pay employees through their separation date, provided they don't resign early, and will share benefits and severance information separately.

Amazon says the closure is part of a $200 million investment to renovate the facility into a new fulfillment center that will reopen in mid-to-late 2028 with approximately 1,000 jobs. Company spokesperson Amber Plunkett said Amazon is working to transfer roughly 850 employees to nearby locations, a figure that doesn't match the roughly 494 workers listed as affected in the WARN filing. The company did not explain how the two numbers relate. Employees have the option to transfer to two nearby facilities specifically, or to any of the company's roughly 30 sites across South Florida. Amazon is offering relocation bonuses to employees who transfer more than 50 miles from Port St. Lucie. All employees affected by the closure will be eligible for rehire once the Port St. Lucie facility reopens.

hero.headline: Flock cameras track rental SUV across Indian River County, lead to Vero Beach burglary arrest
hero.body:
A network of Flock cameras tracked a rental SUV across Indian River County and led deputies to arrest a Vero Beach man accused of burglarizing a home on Reef Road, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.

Guy Keith Tibbetts II, 44, was arrested on Sept. 6 after a homeowner who was out of town saw an unknown man inside his home via surveillance cameras. Footage showed a man wearing an orange long-sleeve shirt, gray shorts, and a blue-and-white cap and gloves arriving at the house a little past 8:30 a.m. Additional footage allegedly showed Tibbetts inside the home with a flashlight and a tote bag, opening drawers, taking a clear acrylic jewelry case, and leaving through the rear sliding door. The items taken were estimated to be valued at around $1,010.

Investigators used the homeowner's description of a small black SUV to search Flock camera data, according to the affidavit. The cameras tracked a black Chevrolet Trailblazer rental vehicle near Reef Road shortly before and after the alleged burglary, then farther west through Indian River County. Deputies were able to track the SUV to Tibbetts' apartment complex.

After being read his rights, Tibbetts allegedly admitted he was the man shown on video and was the only person with access to the rental vehicle. He initially denied entering the home, then admitted he went inside without permission, according to the affidavit. Deputies said a note on his phone, created at 8:45 a.m., listed an address on Reef Road. Tibbetts had also been arrested in August for an alleged Home Depot fraud, and his booking photo matched the suspect in this case, helping deputies identify him. Deputies collected latent prints from the doorbell and rear sliding door. Tibbetts eventually admitted he was the man shown in the surveillance footage, and he was charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling, grand theft between $750 and $5,000, and another theft charge.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce man faces 8 felony charges after admitting to modifying grenades, building destructive device
hero.body:
A Fort Pierce man was charged with eight felony counts after admitting to modifying grenade-like devices and after deputies discovered a homemade destructive device in his home, according to a new arrest affidavit released by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office.

Keith Anthony Morrone allowed St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies to search his vehicle and his Balsam Drive residence after they served him with a temporary risk protection order. Deputies found a green wooden case containing seven items that resembled military style hand grenades. Five of the items were deemed to be more consistent with flash bangs.

While speaking with deputies, Morrone admitted to modifying the grenades, according to the affidavit. When asked if there was anything inside of the grenades, Morrone said I don't know, I don't think there's anything in there, the sheriff's office reported.

After Morrone and everyone else evacuated the residence, the sheriff's office bomb team was called in to handle the situation. The explosives were safely removed from the house. A subsequent search of the home discovered one foot of cannon fuse connected to a small glass container containing black powder, creating a homemade destructive device.

Based on the evidence, Morrone was charged with eight counts of making, possessing, throwing, projecting, placing, or discharging any destructive device or attempting to do so.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce extends King's Landing deadline for $15M Marriott hotel funding
hero.body:
Fort Pierce commissioners voted 3-2 Monday night to give the developer of King's Landing another six months to secure the $15 million it needs to build a planned $65 million Marriott hotel in downtown Fort Pierce. The decision came after a lengthy discussion over whether the city should continue working with developer Live Oak or end the agreement.

Live Oak is planning the Marriott hotel as part of the $200 million King's Landing development. The developer told commissioners it still needs to raise another $15 million to move forward and asked for a six-month extension. Joe Collier, a hotel operating and hospitality partner, said the team will use a different approach to raising the money. "We're going to get in the trenches with Bill and help him raise the money in a different way but need time to do it," Collier said.

Commissioners were divided over the future of the project. The developer has already missed a key deadline under its agreement with the city, prompting some commissioners to push for termination. "This is in material breach," Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said. "We need to stop now because if we do another amendment it continues to weaken us." Commissioner Michael Broderick argued that ending the agreement could create even more delays. "If we pull the plug on this deal now, we're looking at 10 years of turnaround time before we're going to have anything completed over there," Broderick said. "This project is integrally critical to the City of Fort Pierce. We need a downtown hotel. We need more downtown retail."

Community members were also split. "It's time to kick them to the curb," said Howard Dunn Jr. "It's time to move on, cut the losses." Others supported giving the developer another six months. "Let's listen to what they have to say. Six months is not that long," Jamie Hurst said. Fort Pierce resident Charlie Hagg said the community would be delighted to have a Marriott in the city.

A new agreement will be drafted over the next 30 days. Live Oak will then have six months to secure the additional funding needed for the hotel. If the project stays on track, city leaders say construction could begin in roughly one to one-and-a-half years. The planned project would sit along the city's waterfront and is expected to bring millions of dollars in economic activity to the area.

hero.headline: Flock cameras help IRCSO track rental SUV in Vero Beach Reef Road burglary, leading to arrest
hero.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office used Flock camera data to track a rental vehicle and identify a burglary suspect in Vero Beach, leading to the arrest of Guy Keith Tibbetts II on Sept. 6.

Deputies responded after a homeowner who was out of town saw an unknown man inside his Reef Road home via surveillance cameras. Footage showed a man wearing an orange long-sleeve shirt, gray shorts, and a blue-and-white cap and gloves arriving at the house a little past 8:30 a.m. Additional footage allegedly showed the man inside the home with a flashlight and a tote bag, opening drawers, taking a clear acrylic jewelry case, and leaving through the rear sliding door. The stolen items were valued at around $1,010.

Investigators used the homeowner's description of a small black SUV to search Flock camera data. The cameras tracked a black Chevrolet Trailblazer rental vehicle near Reef Road shortly before and after the alleged burglary, then farther west through Indian River County. Deputies were able to track the SUV to an apartment complex where they located Tibbetts, 44. Deputies collected latent prints from the doorbell and rear sliding door.

After being read his rights, Tibbetts allegedly admitted he was the man shown on video and was the only person with access to the rental vehicle. He initially denied entering the home, then admitted he went inside without permission. Deputies said a note on his phone, created at 8:45 a.m., listed an address on Reef Road. Tibbetts had also been arrested in August for an alleged Home Depot fraud, and his booking photo matched the suspect in this case, helping deputies identify him. Tibbetts eventually admitted he was the man shown in the surveillance footage. He was charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling and grand theft between $750 and $5,000, along with another theft charge.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce couple arrested for firing guns while drinking on Happiness Street
hero.body:
A Fort Pierce couple was arrested over the weekend after deputies said they fired multiple weapons into the ground while drinking alcohol outside a residence in the 5100 block of Happiness Street.

Tiffany Lindo and Jacob Mills were taken into custody. St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the individuals had been drinking alcohol before and during the incident. Deputies seized several weapons at the scene, including a shotgun, rifle, and handguns.

Del Toro said discharging a firearm on private property is legal under some circumstances, but the use of alcohol changed the situation. "You can discharge a firearm on your property. It's not recommended, especially in a close-type of residential type neighborhood, but again, when you're mixing alcohol, this could have ended very differently," Del Toro said.

"It would be legal if you weren't using alcohol, but the fact that they were under the influence, that's what made it a second-degree misdemeanor," Del Toro said. The offense could result in up to six months in jail or probation.

Lindo and Mills face charges of discharging a firearm in public or residential area and use of a firearm while under the influence of alcohol. Both have bonded out of jail.

No injuries were reported during the incident. Del Toro said the public is the victim in such situations. "I mean, dealing with a firearm in general can be a dangerous thing; you mix in alcohol, and it can be very dangerous for the people around there," Del Toro said. "So, the public and the state of Florida are the victim, and we have zero tolerance when it comes to doing things like that."

Del Toro issued a warning about mixing firearms and alcohol. "We want to make sure that they're being safe with firearms. You know, I'm very pro-Second Amendment, but at the same time, we have to do things responsibly, and anytime you're using alcohol, please do not use firearms," the sheriff said.

hero.headline: Stuart postpones backyard chicken ordinance vote to next month after staffing issue
hero.body:
The Stuart City Commission postponed a vote Monday night on an ordinance that would allow backyard chickens in certain residential neighborhoods after a key staff member was unable to attend the meeting at the last minute. Commissioners plan to vote on the measure next month.

The ordinance would permit single-family and duplex homes in specific residential areas to keep up to four hens as an accessory use. The proposal was revised to include recommendations from the Community Redevelopment Board, such as standards for fencing, landscaping, and chicken coops. The ordinance was approved in a first reading earlier this year.

Amber D'Angelo, a Martin County resident, said raising hens provides families with benefits such as contributing to more nutritious meals and connecting with food sustainability practices. "Obviously getting to have fresh eggs every day. Getting to promote agriculture and outside learning with your little ones," D'Angelo said. "It's also a property rights issue. I think that people should be able to do what they want on their property, as long as it's not harming anyone."

Some residents and commissioners have raised concerns about potential impacts on water quality and noise. "I'm hoping that the commissioners, the city commissioner majority will, respect people's property rights, respect their constituents, build back trust in this community because recently it's been broken a lot. And I'm hoping that they say yes to backyard chickens as a positive way to build back that bridge of trust," D'Angelo said.

hero.headline: DHS watchdog finds serious health and safety failures at Alligator Alcatraz
hero.body:
A Department of Homeland Security inspector general report found serious health and safety failures at Florida's now-closed Everglades immigration detention center known as Alligator Alcatraz, including the confinement of detainees in small metal enclosures for nearly two hours. Gov. Ron DeSantis defended the operation Monday, saying it helped federal authorities deport people who otherwise could have returned to Florida communities, though he acknowledged he had not read the report.

The federal review followed an unannounced January inspection. Records showed that 79 detainees had been confined in metal enclosures offering about 18 square feet of floor space between July 17, 2025, and January. Stays ranged from several minutes to nearly two hours, with detainees exposed to outdoor temperatures. Inspectors described the practice as unprecedented among detention facilities their office had inspected and a significant risk to detainees' health and safety. Staff described the spaces as calming areas for people seeking time alone. Inspectors also identified an instance in which an enclosure was used after a detainee failed to follow a command.

The review documented insects in bathing areas, showers limited to three times a week and inadequate recreation. Inspectors also found shortcomings in medical care and food service, while finding compliance in the intake and use-of-force areas they reviewed. Staff could not consistently identify which detention standards applied, according to the report. The inspector general administratively closed all 10 recommendations because the facility had ceased operating in June.

Speaking in Lakeland on Monday, DeSantis said the goal had been to exceed federal standards and argued that Florida's assistance was necessary to help carry out the Trump administration's deportation plans. He estimated that Florida's detention assistance helped federal authorities detain and deport about 25,000 people. His remarks referred to both Alligator Alcatraz and a Baker County operation. DeSantis also said the federal government had approved reimbursement for the state's work.

The findings arrive amid a continued fight over the emergency powers and public money used to run the facility. The Florida Division of Emergency Management submitted its overdue spending report Friday, Sept. 11, shortly before lawmakers approved another $250 million for emergency expenses, including immigration costs, according to reporting by The Florida Trib published by WLRN. That report showed Florida had received $84.5 million of an expected $608 million in federal reimbursement for detention centers. It also listed more than $417 million in unpaid immigration-related invoices as of June 30.

Tiffany Lindo and Jacob Mills were taken into custody by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Deputies seized several weapons at the scene, including a shotgun, rifle, and handguns. Both face charges of discharging a firearm in public or residential area and use of a firearm while under the influence of alcohol. Both have bonded out of jail.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the combination of alcohol and firearms led to the charges. He said discharging a firearm on private property is not recommended in close residential neighborhoods, but becomes a second-degree misdemeanor when alcohol is involved.

"You can discharge a firearm on your property. It's not recommended, especially in a close-type of residential type neighborhood, but again, when you're mixing alcohol, this could have ended very differently," Del Toro said. "It would be legal if you weren't using alcohol, but the fact that they were under the influence, that's what made it a second-degree misdemeanor."

Del Toro said the offense could result in up to six months in jail or probation. He emphasized the danger of mixing firearms and alcohol in residential areas.

"I mean, dealing with a firearm in general can be a dangerous thing; you mix in alcohol, and it can be very dangerous for the people around there," Del Toro said. "So, the public and the state of Florida are the victim, and we have zero tolerance when it comes to doing things like that."

No injuries were reported during the incident. The sheriff said he supports Second Amendment rights but stressed the importance of responsible firearm handling.

"We want to make sure that they're being safe with firearms. You know, I'm very pro-Second Amendment, but at the same time, we have to do things responsibly, and anytime you're using alcohol, please do not use firearms," the sheriff said.

cards.headline: Deputies used Flock camera network to track rental SUV, identify Vero Beach burglary suspect
cards.teaser: Indian River County deputies used Flock surveillance cameras to track a rental SUV across the county and identify a man charged with burglarizing a home on Reef Road in Vero Beach.
cards.body:
Indian River County deputies used Flock surveillance cameras to track a rental SUV across the county and identify a man charged with burglarizing a home on Reef Road in Vero Beach, according to an arrest affidavit.

Guy Keith Tibbetts II, 44, was arrested Sept. 6 after deputies investigated the burglary. The homeowner was out of town and saw an unknown man inside his home via his surveillance cameras, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Home surveillance footage showed a man wearing an orange long-sleeve shirt, gray shorts, and a blue-and-white cap and gloves arriving at the house shortly after 8:30 a.m. Additional footage showed the man inside the home with a flashlight and a tote bag, opening drawers, taking a clear acrylic jewelry case, and leaving through the rear sliding door. The stolen items were valued at around $1,010.

Deputies collected latent fingerprints from the doorbell and rear sliding door. Investigators used the homeowner's description of a small black SUV to search Flock camera data, the affidavit said. The cameras tracked a black Chevrolet Trailblazer rental vehicle near Reef Road shortly before and after the burglary, then farther west through Indian River County. Deputies tracked the SUV to Tibbetts' apartment complex.

After being read his rights, Tibbetts admitted he was the man shown on video and was the only person with access to the rental vehicle, according to the affidavit. He initially denied entering the home, then admitted he went inside without permission. Deputies found a note on his phone created at 8:45 a.m. that listed an address on Reef Road. Tibbetts had been arrested in August for an alleged Home Depot fraud, and his booking photo matched the suspect in this case, helping deputies identify him. Tibbetts was charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling, grand theft between $750 and $5,000, and another theft charge.

hero.headline: DHS finds detainees held in metal enclosures at Alligator Alcatraz; DeSantis defends facility
hero.body:
A Department of Homeland Security inspector general report found serious health and safety failures at Florida's now-closed Everglades immigration detention center, including the use of small metal enclosures to hold detainees for nearly two hours. The findings emerged amid an unresolved fight over the $250 million in emergency spending lawmakers approved and more than $417 million in unpaid invoices tied to the state's broader immigration operations.

The federal review followed an unannounced January inspection. Records showed that 79 detainees had been confined in metal enclosures offering about 18 square feet of floor space between July 17, 2025, and January. Stays ranged from several minutes to nearly two hours, with detainees exposed to outdoor temperatures. Inspectors described the practice as unprecedented among detention facilities their office had inspected and a significant risk to detainees' health and safety. Staff described the spaces as calming areas for people seeking time alone. Inspectors also identified an instance in which an enclosure was used after a detainee failed to follow a command.

Gov. Ron DeSantis defended the operation Monday, saying it helped federal authorities deport people who otherwise could have returned to Florida communities. Speaking in Lakeland, DeSantis acknowledged he had not reviewed the findings. He estimated that Florida's detention assistance helped federal authorities detain and deport about 25,000 people, referring to both Alligator Alcatraz and a Baker County operation. DeSantis also said the federal government had approved reimbursement for the state's work.

The review documented insects in bathing areas, showers limited to three times a week and inadequate recreation. Inspectors also found shortcomings in medical care and food service. Staff could not consistently identify which detention standards applied, according to the report. The inspector general administratively closed all 10 recommendations because the facility had ceased operating in June.

The controversy also became a fight over the governor's authority. The Republican-controlled Legislature adopted Senate Bill 7040, which requires quarterly emergency-fund reports covering cash flow, reimbursements, assets and unpaid invoices. The law also subjects spending after emergency renewals to legislative budget review procedures.

FDEM submitted its overdue spending report Friday, Sept. 11, shortly before lawmakers approved another $250 million for emergency expenses, including immigration costs, according to reporting by The Florida Trib published by WLRN. That report showed Florida had received $84.5 million of an expected $608 million in federal reimbursement for detention centers. It also listed more than $417 million in unpaid immigration-related invoices as of June 30. Those figures cover the broader immigration effort, rather than a final accounting of Alligator Alcatraz alone.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce pair who fired guns while drinking face only misdemeanor charges
hero.body:
Two Fort Pierce residents accused of firing multiple guns while drinking in a residential neighborhood face only misdemeanor charges under Florida law, even as a neighbor described bullets flying near his home with his 5-year-old son present.

Tiffany Rose Lindo and Jacob Robert Mills, both 25, were arrested after St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies responded around 9 p.m. Saturday to the 5100 block of Happiness Street following reports of people actively firing guns. Investigators say the pair fired a shotgun, rifle and handguns into the ground and had consumed alcohol before and during the incident. Each faces charges of discharging a firearm in a public or residential area and using a firearm while under the influence of alcohol.

Both charges are misdemeanors under Florida law based on the allegations announced by the Sheriff's Office. The firearm-discharge offense is a first-degree misdemeanor punishable by up to one year in county jail, while using a firearm while impaired by alcohol is a second-degree misdemeanor that can carry up to 60 days in jail. Fort Pierce criminal defense attorney Brian Mallonee said the specific circumstances surrounding where and how a gun is fired determine the charge level. More serious allegations could potentially lead to different charges if a bullet struck a home, vehicle or person, Mallonee said, but prosecutors would still have to prove the elements of the charges.

The neighbor who called 911 told CBS12 News he feared someone was being shot when he heard what he described as a barrage of gunfire Saturday night. He said he heard two gunshots, then a barrage of AR-15 rounds, then shotgun blasts, and then another barrage of AR-15 rounds roughly 300 feet away. The neighbor, who asked that his face not be shown, said his 5-year-old son stays with him every other week. Wood and drywall don't stop bullets, he said. The bullets could've came through the wall and hit my son. No one was injured in the incident. Lindo and Mills have both bonded out of jail, and the Sheriff's Office said the firearms involved were taken as evidence but the pair will have an opportunity to get the guns back once the case is resolved.

Lucie County Sheriff's Office says deputies responded around 9 p.m. 12 to the 5100 block of Happiness Street after reports of people actively firing guns. Deputies identified the two people as Tiffany Rose Lindo and Jacob Robert Mills. Investigators say the pair fired multiple weapons, including a shotgun, rifle and handguns, into the ground. Deputies also said both had consumed alcohol before and during the incident. The neighbor who called 911 spoke with CBS12 News but asked that his face not be shown. I heard two gunshots, he said. And then I heard a barrage of AR-15 rounds, then shotgun, and then a barrage of AR-15 rounds again. See also: Florida driver database hacked through compromised police credentials, state says He said he couldn't tell where the bullets were going or exactly what was happening roughly 300 feet away. It kind of freaked me out a little bit, just not knowing what direction or where they were shooting, he said. Wood and drywall don't stop bullets. The concern was especially personal. The neighbor said his 5-year-old son stays with him every other week. The bullets could've came through the wall and hit my son, he said. Why are the charges misdemeanors? Lindo and Mills were each arrested on charges of discharging a firearm in a public or residential area and using a firearm while under the influence of alcohol. Despite the potential danger described by the neighbor, both charges are misdemeanors under Florida law based on the allegations announced by the Sheriff's Office. CBS12 News asked Fort Pierce criminal defense attorney Brian Mallonee why the alleged conduct does not automatically result in a felony. You'd have to ask your lawmakers that, Mallonee said. That would be a question for the guys in Tallahassee. Mallonee explained that Florida's firearm-discharge law includes specific circumstances surrounding where and how a gun is fired. The size of a property and density of the surrounding residential area can matter, but he said negligently or recklessly firing a weapon can be illegal regardless of property size. The firearm-discharge offense can be a first-degree misdemeanor, punishable by up to one year in county jail. Mallonee said any eventual sentence would depend on factors including a defendant's prior record and how reckless or negligent the conduct was. Florida also separately prohibits using a firearm while impaired by alcohol or certain controlled substances. That offense is a second-degree misdemeanor, which can carry up to 60 days in jail. Mallonee said allegations involving alcohol could also factor into questions about whether someone's handling or discharge of a firearm was negligent or reckless. However, prosecutors would still have to prove the elements of the charges. More serious allegations could potentially lead to different charges if a bullet struck a home, vehicle or person, Mallonee said. In this case, the Sheriff's Office said no one was injured. The neighbor said that's what matters most. If you're gonna be drinking, don't touch a gun, he said. Because you don't know where the bullet's gonna end up. Lindo and Mills have both bonded out of jail. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office tells CBS12 News the firearms involved were taken as evidence, but the pair will have an opportunity to get the guns back once the case is resolved.

hero.headline: Martin County High School evacuated after second bomb threat this month
hero.body:
Students and staff at Martin County High School were evacuated Monday afternoon after a bomb threat prompted a response from the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The incident marks the second bomb threat reported at the school this month, raising concerns among parents and school staff as authorities continue investigating.

In a message sent to families, school officials said all buildings were being evacuated at the direction of law enforcement while authorities investigate the threat. "We are currently evacuating all buildings under the direction of the Martin County Sheriff's Office due to a bomb threat. The safety of our students and staff remains our highest priority," school officials said.

No injuries have been reported.

School leaders thanked families for their patience and cooperation during the evacuation and emphasized that student and staff safety remains the top priority. The school said it is working closely with law enforcement and will continue to provide updates as more information becomes available. The Martin County Sheriff's Office is expected to provide further information as the investigation continues.

cards.headline: Old Havana Cafe, House of Hope set world record with 400-foot Cuban sandwich in Palm City
cards.teaser: Old Havana Cafe and House of Hope built a 400-foot Cuban sandwich Saturday morning in Palm City, breaking the previous world record held by Tampa and raising more than $30,000 for local programs.
cards.body:
Old Havana Cafe and House of Hope built a 400-foot Cuban sandwich Saturday morning in Palm City, breaking the previous world record held by Tampa. The event raised more than $30,000 for House of Hope, a Martin County nonprofit that provides food assistance, job training, education and other services aimed at helping local families become more self-sufficient.

A large crowd turned out to watch volunteers and sandwich builders assemble the record-breaking Cuban sandwich and support the fundraiser. Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi was on hand to complete the final measurement confirming the sandwich reached 400 feet.

Organizers said the event was about more than setting a world record. The event was designed to bring the community together while raising awareness and support for House of Hope's mission.

Martin County is now home to the world's longest Cuban sandwich.

hero.headline: Florida highway agency confirms data breach by international criminals using Plant City police login
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles confirmed Friday that an international criminal organization breached state systems on Sept. 4 using a Plant City police employee's login credentials that were improperly stored on a personal device.

The department said the breach was quickly stopped and no further intrusion has occurred. Officials did not identify the criminal group or say how many drivers were affected or what information was exposed.

The FLHSMV is working with the Florida Digital Service and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement on the investigation. The department said it will release more information later as the criminal investigation continues.

hero.headline: Four bomb threats hit Treasure Coast in eight days; police probe Russia link
hero.body:
Fort Pierce police and the FBI are investigating four bomb threats reported across the Treasure Coast over the last eight days, including a Saturday threat that evacuated visitor areas at HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce. Three of the four threats were sent by email, and investigators are working to determine whether the incidents are connected.

Police cruisers surrounded Lawnwood Hospital Saturday afternoon as officers searched the building after receiving an emailed threat. Visitor areas were evacuated as a precaution, and police gave the all-clear several hours later. Patient care was not interrupted. Police said the threat followed similar patterns to a threat reported Friday at Indian River State College and threats made at two Treasure Coast area high schools.

The first threat was called in at Fort Pierce Central High School on Friday, September 4. Students were evacuated while deputies investigated. Investigators said the email address used to send the threat to Martin County High School had been hacked and may have been connected to a suspect in Russia. None of the threats were found to be credible, but officers continue to take each one seriously. No explosives were found in any of the incidents.

Major Michael Santiago with the Fort Pierce Police Department said investigators will continue working to identify whoever is behind the threats. "Once we narrow this down, those who are making these threats, we will find you and we will prosecute you," Santiago said. Dan Toback, who lives in Port St. Lucie and runs a community news page called SLC Scanner, said the threats are creating unnecessary fear in the community. "These threats that are coming out are people that are simply trying to cause fear, nothing more," Toback said. All four incidents remain under investigation. Police are asking anyone with information about the threats to contact investigators.

cards.body:
Two Fort Pierce residents were arrested after St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies responded to reports of people actively discharging firearms at a residence on Happiness Street on Sept. 12.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce man arrested after eight explosive devices found at Balsam Drive home
hero.body:
Keith Anthony Morrone, 57, of Fort Pierce, was arrested and charged with eight counts of explosives, possessing, making or attempting to make destructive devices after investigators found eight improvised explosive devices and bomb-making materials at his home in the 6000 block of Balsam Drive, the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said Friday.

Morrone is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on a $20,000 bond. Eight firearms were also taken into custody pursuant to the service of a risk protection order.

At approximately 12:20 p.m. Thursday, detectives with the SLCSO Targeted Violence Unit were serving a risk protection order at the residence when they identified suspected destructive devices, Fort Pierce police said in a news release Friday morning. Detectives secured the residence and surrounding area and requested assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Bomb Disposal Team.

Bomb technicians responded to the residence and conducted a preliminary examination of the suspected devices. Technicians removed seven devices from the residence and safely secured them in a containment vessel. Detectives subsequently obtained a search warrant for the residence. During the execution of the search warrant, investigators located an additional improvised explosive device, which was safely secured and removed. Investigators also found a large quantity of materials used in the construction of explosive devices.

"This investigation underscores the seriousness of what our detectives encountered and the importance of being alert to the threats around us," Sheriff Richard Del Toro said. "Our Targeted Violence Unit detectives recognized the potential danger and took immediate action, and our Bomb Disposal Team technicians put themselves in harm's way to safely secure and remove these devices. I'm proud of their professionalism and courage, and grateful for the expertise and partnership of the FBI and ATF as we continue this investigation."

The investigation remains ongoing, and there is no immediate threat to the community.

Terry Rates, who has lived in the neighborhood for 10 years, described the area as peaceful and said he was surprised to see such activity near his home. "It's a really nice neighborhood. That's the first I've ever heard of anything happening around here," he said.

hero.headline: Fourth bomb threat in two weeks targets Lawnwood Hospital; FBI joins probe
hero.body:
A bomb threat emailed to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital on Saturday marked the fourth such threat made via email in less than two weeks on the Treasure Coast. Fort Pierce police are now working with the FBI to track down the source.

Police learned an email was sent just before 11 a.m. Saturday alleging two bombs were planted inside the hospital. The Fort Pierce Police Department mobilized and partially evacuated the facility. A spokesperson for HCA said patient care was not impacted, and visitors were asked to wait outside while police swept the two areas mentioned in the threat. Authorities ultimately determined the threat was not credible.

Fort Pierce police said Saturday's threat was similar in nature to a threat made at nearby Indian River State College earlier this week, as well as two threats at Treasure Coast area high schools. Law enforcement responded to Fort Pierce Central High School last week. Parent Angela Jones described her reaction when she learned there was a threat. "I was concerned. I was like, what's going on? I got a phone call from the school stating that it was a bomb threat," Jones said. On Thursday, a similar situation unfolded at Martin County High School. Nothing was found at any of the campuses. Police said all of the recent incidents are being investigated holistically.

Former State Attorney for Palm Beach County Dave Aronberg said law enforcement is getting better at tracking down suspects in these cases, even when jurisdictional issues arise depending on where a threat originated. "They have a lot of advanced tools who can, that can track people and find out through IP addresses and other means. They can issue subpoenas," Aronberg said. Aronberg also outlined the serious legal consequences for anyone found responsible. "Florida law makes it a 2nd-degree felony to compose and send any written or electronic record that includes emails or text messages that threaten to kill or do bodily injury or conduct a mass shooting or an act of terrorism. So you're talking about a serious felony punishment of up to 15 years in prison," Aronberg said.

hero.headline: Fourth bomb threat in under two weeks forces partial evacuation at HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital
hero.body:
A bomb threat emailed to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital on Saturday forced a partial evacuation of the facility and marked the fourth such threat made via email in less than two weeks on the Treasure Coast. Fort Pierce police are now working with the FBI to track down the source.

Police learned an email was sent just before 11 a.m. Saturday alleging two bombs were planted inside the hospital. The Fort Pierce Police Department mobilized and partially evacuated the facility. A spokesperson for HCA said patient care was not impacted, and visitors were asked to wait outside while police swept the two areas mentioned in the threat. Authorities ultimately determined the threat was not credible.

Fort Pierce police said Saturday's threat was similar in nature to a threat made at nearby Indian River State College earlier this week, as well as two threats at Treasure Coast area high schools. Fort Pierce Central High School received a threat last week, followed by a similar situation at Martin County High School on Thursday. Nothing was found at any of the campuses. Police said all of the recent incidents are being investigated holistically.

Former State Attorney for Palm Beach County Dave Aronberg said law enforcement is getting better at tracking down suspects in these cases, even when jurisdictional issues arise depending on where a threat originated. "They have a lot of advanced tools who can, that can track people and find out through IP addresses and other means. They can issue subpoenas," Aronberg said. Aronberg also outlined the serious legal consequences for anyone found responsible. "Florida law makes it a 2nd-degree felony to compose and send any written or electronic record that includes emails or text messages that threaten to kill or do bodily injury or conduct a mass shooting or an act of terrorism. So you're talking about a serious felony punishment of up to 15 years in prison," Aronberg said.

Angela Jones, a parent at Fort Pierce Central High School, described her reaction when she learned there was a threat. "I was concerned. I was like, what's going on? I got a phone call from the school stating that it was a bomb threat," Jones said.

cards.headline: Two Fort Pierce residents arrested after firing weapons at Happiness Street residence

St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies arrested two Fort Pierce residents after responding to reports of people actively discharging firearms at a residence in the 5100 block of Happiness Street on Sept. 12.

Deputies responded at approximately 9 p.m. following reports of gunfire. A witness reported seeing a man and a woman firing multiple weapons, including a shotgun, rifle and handguns. Deputies determined the subjects were firing the weapons into the ground. Investigators learned both subjects had been consuming alcohol before and during the incident.

Tiffany Rose Lindo, 25, and Jacob Roibert Mills, 25, both of Fort Pierce, were each arrested and charged with discharging a firearm in a public or residential area and use of a firearm while under the influence of alcohol. No one was injured.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie honors 25th anniversary of 9/11 with remembrance ceremony
cards.teaser: Community members, city leaders and first responders gathered Friday morning at the MIDFLORIDA Event Center memorial to mark 25 years since the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie held its annual 9/11 Remembrance Ceremony Friday morning at the Memorial Fountain at the MIDFLORIDA Event Center, marking the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. Community members, city leaders and first responders gathered to honor the victims and survivors of the 2001 tragedy.

Mayor Shannon Martin, Police Chief Leo Niemczyk, St. Lucie County Fire District Firefighter/Paramedic Allen Civita and other local public safety leaders took part in the ceremony. Retired New York City Police Department detective Rafael Diaz served as the guest speaker, and the Port St. Lucie High School Choir performed.

Port St. Lucie resident Michael Cozzolino said the anniversary brought back memories of watching the attacks unfold while he was in Florida for work. "I remember I was living in Connecticut at the time, I was here in Florida, had no way back, just a rental car, and we all piled in a rental car and drove back," Cozzolino said. "I'll never forget that day." Cozzolino said the uncertainty in the hours after the attacks was frightening. "Especially being a defense contractor. Don't know where they're going to hit next," he said.

Cozzolino, a member of the Nam Knights Motorcycle Club of America, said the anniversary remains especially emotional for many first responders and veterans. "We have 84 chapters in the United States. We have 16 here, 17 here alone in Florida. About 1,400 members," Cozzolino said. "A lot of them were from New York. So, a lot of first responders, and a lot of them have the cancer now." Cozzolino said seeing the community gather at the memorial was meaningful. "The way they do this, they have the steel flowers, flags. Very patriotic here," Cozzolino said. "This town's very diverse town, and it's a great town to live in." The Port St. Lucie ceremony was one of several events across the region marking the 25th anniversary of the attacks.

hero.headline: Palm City sets world record with 400-foot Cuban sandwich to fight food insecurity
hero.body:
Community members in Palm City built a 400-foot Cuban sandwich at Justin Wilson Memorial Park on Sandpiper Way, setting a world record and raising funds for House of Hope, a nonprofit that serves more than 30,000 Martin County residents facing hunger each month.

The previous record was 365 feet, set in Tampa in 2024. The event, called Bite Into History: The Longest Cuban Sandwich Ever Made, was a joint effort of Old Havana Cafe at 2225 SE Ocean Blvd. and House of Hope. Organizers said the event was intended to call attention to food insecurity, foster community spirit and celebrate Hispanic heritage. Members of the public could purchase sandwiches.

The Doris M. Carter Family Foundation, the event's presenting sponsor, pledged to match every donation made through the event up to $15,000, doubling every donor's impact in the community.

Founded in 1984, House of Hope empowers Martin County residents to overcome hunger and hardship. The organization helps with basic needs such as food, clothing, furniture and financial assistance, as well as longer-term case management services. House of Hope has service centers in Stuart, Hobe Sound, Indiantown and Jensen Beach, with thrift stores in Stuart, Hobe Sound and Indiantown. The organization also operates the Growing Hope Farm in Palm City and several nutrition gardens that provide sustainable sources of fresh produce for clients as well as nutrition education and vocational opportunities to the community.

A Cuban sandwich is ham, roasted pork, Swiss cheese, pickles, mustard and sometimes salami on Cuban bread. Tampa and Miami have a rivalry over which city claims the sandwich as its own. In 2012, the Tampa City Council named it the city's official signature sandwich. Around the 1900s, cafes in Ybor City and nearby West Tampa sold the sandwiches to immigrant workers who were part of the cigar factories. By the 1960s, Cuban sandwiches were common in Miami with a large influx of Cuban residents after Fidel Castro's 1959 rise to power in their native land.

hero.headline: Fourth bomb threat in under two weeks prompts Lawnwood Hospital evacuation
hero.body:
A bomb threat emailed to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital Saturday marked the fourth such threat made via email in less than two weeks on the Treasure Coast. Fort Pierce police are now working with the FBI to track down the source.

Police learned an email was sent just before 11 a.m. Saturday alleging two bombs were planted inside the hospital. The Fort Pierce Police Department mobilized and partially evacuated the facility. A hospital spokesperson said patient care was not impacted, and visitors were asked to wait outside while police swept the two areas mentioned in the threat. Authorities ultimately determined the threat was not credible.

Fort Pierce police said Saturday's threat was similar in nature to a threat made at Indian River State College earlier this week, as well as two threats at Treasure Coast area high schools. Fort Pierce Central High School received a threat last week. Parent Angela Jones described her reaction when she learned there was a threat. "I was concerned. I was like, what's going on? I got a phone call from the school stating that it was a bomb threat," Jones said. On Thursday, a similar situation unfolded at Martin County High School. Nothing was found at any of the campuses. Police said all of the recent incidents are being investigated holistically.

Former State Attorney for Palm Beach County Dave Aronberg said law enforcement is getting better at tracking down suspects in these cases, even when jurisdictional issues arise depending on where a threat originated. "They have a lot of advanced tools who can, that can track people and find out through IP addresses and other means. They can issue subpoenas," Aronberg said. Aronberg also outlined the serious legal consequences for anyone found responsible. "Florida law makes it a 2nd-degree felony to compose and send any written or electronic record that includes emails or text messages that threaten to kill or do bodily injury or conduct a mass shooting or an act of terrorism. So you're talking about a serious felony punishment of up to 15 years in prison," Aronberg said.

cards.headline: Man arrested after bomb squad removes 8 improvised explosives from Fort Pierce home
cards.teaser: Detectives serving a risk protection order at a residence in the 6000 block of Balsam Drive discovered suspected destructive devices, prompting a bomb squad response and the removal of eight improvised explosive devices.
cards.body:
Keith Anthony Morrone, 57, of Fort Pierce, was arrested and charged with eight counts of explosives, possessing, making or attempting to make destructive devices after detectives discovered improvised explosive devices at his residence in the 6000 block of Balsam Drive. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office arrested Morrone following an investigation that began Thursday. Morrone is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on a $20,000 bond.

At approximately 12:20 p.m. Thursday, detectives with the SLCSO Targeted Violence Unit were serving a risk protection order at the residence when they identified suspected destructive devices, Fort Pierce police said in a news release Friday morning. Detectives secured the residence and surrounding area and requested assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Bomb Disposal Team.

Bomb technicians conducted a preliminary examination of the suspected devices and removed seven devices from the residence, safely securing them in a containment vessel. Detectives subsequently obtained a search warrant for the residence. During the execution of the search warrant, investigators located an additional improvised explosive device, which was safely secured and removed. This brought the total number of improvised explosive devices recovered from the residence to eight.

Investigators also found a large quantity of materials used in the construction of explosive devices. Eight firearms were also taken into custody pursuant to the service of a risk protection order. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the Targeted Violence Unit detectives recognized the potential danger and took immediate action. The investigation remains ongoing.

Terry Rates, who has lived in the neighborhood for 10 years, told WPBF's Ari Hait he was surprised to see such activity near his home. Rates described the area as peaceful. "It's a really nice neighborhood. That's the first I've ever heard of anything happening around here," he said.

cards.headline: Two Fort Pierce residents arrested for firing weapons into ground while intoxicated
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County deputies arrested two people after they fired multiple weapons into the ground while drinking alcohol on Happiness Street in Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies arrested two Fort Pierce residents after responding to reports of people actively discharging firearms at a residence on Happiness Street on Sept.

Deputies responded at approximately 9 p.m. to the 5100 block of Happiness Street following the reports. A witness reported seeing a man and a woman firing multiple weapons, including a shotgun, rifle and handguns.

Deputies determined the subjects were firing the weapons into the ground. Investigators learned both subjects had been consuming alcohol before and during the incident. The individuals were identified as Tiffany Rose Lindo, 25, and Jacob Roibert Mills, 25, both of Fort Pierce. Lindo and Mills were each charged with discharging a firearm in a public or residential area and use of a firearm while under the influence of alcohol. No one was injured.

A hospital spokesperson confirmed there was a temporary evacuation of visitors. Patient care was never impacted, the spokesperson said.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie 9/11 ceremony draws first responders, residents 25 years later
cards.teaser: Community members, city leaders and first responders gathered Friday morning at the MIDFLORIDA Event Center to honor victims and survivors of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks on the 25th anniversary of the tragedy.
cards.body:
Community members, city leaders and first responders gathered Friday morning at the MIDFLORIDA Event Center in Port St. Lucie to honor victims and survivors of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks on the 25th anniversary of the tragedy. The city's annual 9/11 Remembrance Ceremony was held at the Memorial Fountain at the MIDFLORIDA Event Center.

Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin, Police Chief Leo Niemczyk, St. Lucie County Fire District Firefighter/Paramedic Allen Civita and other local public safety leaders took part in the ceremony. Retired New York City Police Department detective Rafael Diaz served as guest speaker, and the Port St. Lucie High School Choir performed.

Port St. Lucie resident Michael Cozzolino said the anniversary brought back memories of watching the attacks unfold while he was in Florida for work. "I remember I was living in Connecticut at the time, I was here in Florida, had no way back, just a rental car, and we all piled in a rental car and drove back," Cozzolino said. "I'll never forget that day." Cozzolino said the uncertainty in the hours after the attacks was frightening. "Especially being a defense contractor. Don't know where they're going to hit next," he said.

Cozzolino said seeing the community gather at the memorial was meaningful. "The way they do this, they have the steel flowers, flags. Very patriotic here," Cozzolino said. "This town's very diverse town, and it's a great town to live in." Cozzolino, a member of the Nam Knights Motorcycle Club of America, said the anniversary remains especially emotional for many first responders and veterans. "We have 84 chapters in the United States. We have 16 here, 17 here alone in Florida. About 1,400 members," Cozzolino said. "A lot of them were from New York. So, a lot of first responders, and a lot of them have the cancer now." The Port St. Lucie ceremony was one of several events across the region marking the 25th anniversary of the attacks.
